title: The French QUE
kidRule: In words that came to us from French, Q-U can say a plain K, with no 'kw' sound at all. At the end of a word that K sound is spelled Q-U-E, as in PLAQUE and TECHNIQUE!
hint: Listen for a K sound. In this French word it is not spelled with a K or with C-K! Which letters make it?
reminder: The K sound here is spelled the French way: Q-U, and Q-U-E at the end of a word.

check.question: Why does PLAQUE end with Q-U-E?
check.correctAnswer: Because it came from French, where a K sound at the end is spelled Q-U-E!
distractors: Because Q and U always say 'kw' together
Because every word with a Q in it has to end with an E

words.def: A flat sign, often made of metal or stone, that tells about a special person or place.
words.sent: A shiny plaque on the wall tells who built our school.
words.story: The Apollo 11 astronauts left a plaque on the Moon. It says, 'We came in peace for all mankind'!
words.card: The *plaque* in the *pla*yground says, 'A very brave worm lived here!'

words.def: A special way of doing something that takes skill.
words.sent: The art teacher showed us a new technique for painting clouds.
words.story: The word comes from the Greek word 'techne', which means art or skill!
words.card: My high-*tech* robot has a secret *technique* for flipping pancakes!

words.def: A building where Muslims go to pray.
words.sent: The mosque has a blue dome and a tall tower.
words.story: The Great Mosque of Djenne in Mali, Africa, is the largest mud-brick building in the world!
words.card: A *mos*sy green frog sat quietly in the garden of the *mosque*!

words.def: Not see-through, so that light cannot shine through it.
words.sent: The bathroom window is opaque, so nobody can see in.
words.story: A glass frog is the opposite of opaque: the skin on its tummy is so clear that you can see its heart beating!
words.card: The *pa*nda painted the window *opaque* so nobody could see him eating cake!

words.def: A lawn game where you hit wooden balls through little hoops with a long hammer called a mallet.
words.sent: We played croquet on the grass after lunch.
words.story: In the book Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Queen plays croquet using flamingos as mallets and hedgehogs as balls!
words.card: A *cro*w won the *croquet* game by rolling the ball with its beak!

words.def: To win against something hard, like a fear or a tall mountain.
words.sent: She was proud to conquer her fear of the deep end of the pool.
words.story: In 1953 Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay became the first people known to conquer Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth!
words.card: The fal*con* helped me *conquer* the giant mountain of laundry!

words.sent: We stopped at a picturesque village with flowers in every window.
words.story: The word came from the Italian 'pittoresco', which means 'the way a painter would do it'!
words.card: Take a *picture*! This *picturesque* pond has a duck in a bow tie!

words.def: A careful look at a piece of work that tells what is good about it and what could be better.
words.sent: My teacher wrote a kind critique of my story.
words.story: The word comes from the Greek 'kritikos', which means 'able to judge'!
words.card: A furry *crit*ter gave my mud pie a glowing *critique*!

words.def: The polite way to behave, like saying please and thank you.
words.sent: Good etiquette means waiting until everyone is served before you eat.
words.story: In French this word also means 'label'. The English word 'ticket' comes from the very same old French word!
words.card: The y*eti* has perfect *etiquette*: he always says, 'Please pass the snowballs!'

words.def: The shape and strength of a person's body.
words.sent: The swimmer has a strong physique from years of practice.
words.story: It comes from the Greek word 'physis', which means nature. The words physics and physical belong to the same family!
words.card: Our *phys*ical education teacher showed off his *physique* by lifting a giant pumpkin!
